tagline: Prairie and farmland along US 75, carrying an old auto-trail name.
intro: Prairie and farmland accompany US 75 along Minnesota’s western edge, with few large towns along the way. Explore Minnesota presents the King of Trails Scenic Byway through its gentle prairie scenery, community history, national monument and state parks.

The King of Trails was an early auto trail, a road known by a name before numbered highways took over. In Minnesota, that name gave way to the trunk highway system commissioned in 1920. Towns along the route later brought the name back by sponsoring the Historic King of Trails designation for Minnesota’s stretch of US 75.

Heading north from the Iowa line, US 75 enters Minnesota south of Luverne and continues through Pipestone. At Lake Benton, the route reaches a town on Buffalo Ridge beside its namesake lake. At Breckenridge, the Bois de Sioux and Otter Tail join to form the Red River of the North. Around Moorhead, the land is flat farmland on the bed of glacial Lake Agassiz. Beyond Moorhead, US 75 angles northeast through Crookston, then northwest toward the river. The road ends at Noyes; its crossing into Canada closed in 2006, leaving the inspection station standing beside a dead end.
notice: At Noyes, the former US inspection station survives beside the highway’s dead end.

moments.title: Pipestone National Monument
moments.text: Indigenous people continue quarrying Pipestone’s red stone for pipes used in prayer and ceremony, a practice extending back more than 3,000 years. Reaching it means breaking through several feet of quartzite, work that can take days or stretch into years. The quarry tract also became the subject of a fight over ownership. In 1926, the Supreme Court held that the Yankton Sioux Tribe owned the 648-acre tract and was owed just compensation because the United States had taken it. The monument now consults with 23 Tribal Nations, while Indigenous people from across the country keep quarrying traditions alive.
moments.notice: The three-quarter-mile self-guided trail offers views of the pipestone quarries and a waterfall.

moments.title: Breckenridge
moments.text: Two rivers become a third at Breckenridge and its twin city, Wahpeton, North Dakota. The Bois de Sioux and Otter Tail meet here to form the Red River of the North, which flows toward Manitoba and Lake Winnipeg. On that northward journey, the river forms most of the boundary between Minnesota and North Dakota. Breckenridge also stood on the Great Northern Railway’s main line between the Twin Cities and Seattle. Passenger trains served its station until 1979. Freight trains continue to use the line under BNSF, while US 75 remains one of the city’s main roads.
moments.notice: The Bois de Sioux and Otter Tail meet here to become the north-flowing Red River.

moments.title: Noyes
moments.text: In 1931, the United States built Noyes’s large inspection station at one of the busiest border crossings west of the Great Lakes. US 75 replaced the Jefferson Highway here, carrying road traffic across to Emerson, Manitoba. Then Interstate 29 and newer facilities at Pembina and West Lynne drew most vehicles away. Canada closed its station in 2003. Only US-bound traffic continued until 2006, when the United States closed its port and the connecting road was permanently barricaded. The 1931 US station still stands, listed in the National Register of Historic Places; the adjacent rail crossing remains in operation.
moments.notice: The road between the former border stations is permanently barricaded.

practical: Noyes: US 75 does not cross into Canada at Noyes. Cross-border road traffic must use the Pembina–Emerson crossing. (checked 2026-10-11)
